title: The Guardian view on Labour and the Greens: winning trust takes more than words | Editorial
content: A byelection win is a fillip for Andy Burnham and shows Zack Polanski must confront the failures damaging his party’s credibility and appeal By holding Holborn and St Pancras, Andy Burnham’s Labour has shown it can attract liberal and left-leaning voters. The seat has substantial numbers of young adults, students, professionals and Muslims – offering fertile ground for the Greens’ ecopopulism. However, Labour prevailed. Having won leave-voting Makerfield in June, Mr Burnham can now claim an appeal that bridges Labour’s divided electorate. It’s worth noting that turnout in London was low and Labour’s vote share fell 3.7 points. But that compares with an average 19.3-point fall in four byelections under Mr Burnham’s predecessor. The new leader clearly has bought Labour breathing space and checked the Green advance. The Greens more than tripled their vote share in the constituency to 33%. But they were beaten. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% in Sir Keir Starmer’s former seat, leaving Zack Polanski’s ambition of entering parliament unfulfilled. For a party that began the year promising to turn voters’ hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, this was a sobering moment. The passing of a motion declaring “Zionism is racism” at its conference probably cost the party support – though the result in central London alone cannot definitively say that. There is a separate question of leadership. Mr Polanski now says he would have voted against the motion. Why, then, did he not make his opposition clear when it mattered last weekend? He intends to remain leader – and the expanded, radical membership has given Mr Polanski a base in the party that likely insulates him from an instant coup. But with calls for his resignation growing, he has to try to stay in the job while restoring confidence in the Greens’ electoral chances. Clouds had emerged on the horizon long before the party’s conference. Its spring polling surge has faded. In March, YouGov put the party second nationally to Reform, on 21%. Mr Burnham has since stolen much of the Greens’ rhetorical thunder by consciously evoking a more leftwing agenda. The party is now in fourth place, polling 10% nationally. As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents. Since the beginning of the year his net favourability rating has fallen from -6 to -29. The Greens are not to be discounted. Mr Burnham has yet to turn hope into lasting support. That will depend on what his government delivers, especially as prices rise, rather than whom it defeats. In an interview with the BBC, Jonathan Bartley, the Greens’ former party co-leader, warned that the influx of members has changed the party and that some newcomers are unaware of its traditions of consensus and opposition to political “purity tests”. Significantly, Mr Polanski’s deputy, Rachel Millward, said that the party structures needed to become “fully democratic and strategic”. This may not be enough for the Green MP Siân Berry, who said she wanted to “fix the serious flaws” in the controversial Zionism motion. Leadership is missing, and responsibility for that falls squarely on Mr Polanski. He has shown that he can communicate persuasively. Now, if he remains in post, he must show that he can acknowledge what went wrong and build support for changing the controversial Zionism policy. Mr Polanski claims credit for Labour’s leftward turn. But the Green leader now needs to put his own party’s house in order. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: Labour's recent byelection victory against the Greens highlights Andy Burnham's ability to unite a divided electorate, while exposing the internal policy failures and declining public trust facing Green leader Zack Polanski.
skimming: Labour's byelection victory in Holborn and St Pancras checked the growing electoral momentum of the Green Party.
The Greens faced setbacks due to controversial conference motions and a steep decline in national polling numbers.
Zack Polanski's leadership favorability has significantly dropped, prompting internal calls for reform and accountability.
To rebuild credibility, the Green leadership must fix internal structural flaws and address controversial policies rather than rely on rhetoric.

title: The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted | Editorial
content: More research into the troubling rise in early onset cancers is needed. But we already know that food is among the culprits The latest findings about the rise in cancers in people under 50, from the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), are extremely concerning. While a cancer diagnosis is bad news at any time, it is a particular blow for those in younger age groups where most people are in good health. Overlapping trends observed in England, the Netherlands and the US include a troubling rise in the incidence of colorectal (or bowel) cancer. Other diseases that have increased in England include uterine and kidney cancers. These diseases are still rare in young people: 10 times more adults in their 50s, 60s and 70s are diagnosed than those in their 20s, 30s and 40s. Earlier detection is thought to be one factor behind the rise in younger patients. Diagnosing more cancers sooner is an explicit policy goal in England, where late diagnosis and lower uptake of screening are two reasons for mortality rates that are higher than elsewhere in Europe. But diagnostic improvements are unfortunately not the main reason for increased cases. While research is ongoing and many questions remain, evidence points to obesity and poor diet causing cancers as well as heart disease and type 2 diabetes. The Prospect-UK trial is currently seeking 250,000 participants for a longitudinal study into early-onset (under-50) bowel cancer. It will scrutinise information about nutrition in more detail than has been done previously, including what people are eating less of. The success of international efforts to cut lung cancer through targeting smoking set a powerful precedent for public health campaigning. This took longer than it should have done, due to tobacco industry lobbying. But it remains the gold standard of regulation combined with messaging, to bring about behaviour change. The WCRF data shows that lung cancer rates in under-50s have continued falling. So far, efforts to cut obesity have had nothing like the same impact. The patterns are not the same everywhere; one recent study found that in some countries a rapid rise had been replaced by a levelling-off. But English-speaking countries have some of the worst records, and the lack of strong action in the UK is among the big disappointments of health policy in the last decade. Politicians from Boris Johnson to Wes Streeting have committed to obesity action plans, only to water them down in the face of opposition from the food and drink industries. Last year, scientists wrote to Mr Streeting to protest that the government had done “virtually nothing” to alert consumers to the carcinogenic properties of the nitrites added to bacon and ham. There is a grim irony in dramatic advances in cancer research and treatment coinciding with the rise in early-onset cancers. For many doctors and patients, this a period of hope. But politicians and health bosses must guard against a situation in which some groups have improved prospects, while others face increased risks linked to socioeconomic disadvantages. In relation to obesity and diet, the close link with poverty points to the need for ministers to view public spending holistically, and to recognise that the NHS is not the only institution with the capacity to improve health. While more research into early-onset cancers is needed, existing data tells us a great deal. Governments should be as bold in tackling the causes of obesity as they once were in confronting big tobacco. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: The rising incidence of early-onset cancers among under-50s is increasingly linked to obesity and poor diet, necessitating bold government intervention and regulation of the food industry akin to historical anti-tobacco campaigns.
skimming: Early-onset cancers, particularly colorectal, uterine, and kidney cancers, are rising alarmingly among people under 50.
While diagnostic improvements help detect cases early, obesity and poor nutrition are identified as the primary drivers of this trend.
The historical success of anti-smoking campaigns serves as a gold standard for how public health regulations can successfully drive behavioral change.
UK policymakers have repeatedly watered down anti-obesity measures due to food industry lobbying, highlighting the urgent need for holistic, poverty-focused interventions.
grammar: The text uses the 'only to + infinitive' structure ('...only to water them down...'), which is a common grammatical device used to express a frustrating, disappointing, or unexpected subsequent event or result.
